questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Endocrine Glands and Hormones' refers to.
questions.a: Chemical substances that function as messengers between cells, are not used as nutrients, and are synthesized in minute quantities by ductless glands.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Endocrine Glands and Hormones'.
questions.a: Hormones provide a slow but long-lasting coordination system compared to the rapid neural system.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Endocrine Glands and Hormones' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.1 (source: kebo119.txt lines 10-35)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Hypothalamus' refers to.
questions.a: The basal part of the forebrain that contains neurosecretory cells which form hormones to regulate the pituitary gland.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Hypothalamus'.
questions.a: The hypothalamus links the nervous system to the endocrine system via releasing and inhibiting hormones.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Hypothalamus' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.2.1 (source: kebo119.txt lines 55-80)

concepts.title: The Pituitary Gland and Growth Disorders

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Pituitary Gland and Growth Disorders' refers to.
questions.a: A master gland located in the sella tursica that secretes several trophic hormones and stores hypothalamic hormones.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Pituitary Gland and Growth Disorders'.
questions.a: The pituitary regulates growth, milk production, and the activity of other endocrine glands.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Pituitary Gland and Growth Disorders' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.2.2 (source: kebo119.txt lines 85-120)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Thyroid Gland and Metabolism' refers to.
questions.a: A two-lobed gland in the neck that produces thyroxine and triiodothyronine to regulate the body's basal metabolic rate.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Thyroid Gland and Metabolism'.
questions.a: Iodine is necessary for thyroid hormone synthesis, which controls nutrient metabolism and RBC formation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Thyroid Gland and Metabolism' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.2.4 (source: kebo119.txt lines 150-185)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Parathyroid Gland and Calcium Balance' refers to.
questions.a: Four small glands on the thyroid's back that secrete parathyroid hormone (PTH) to increase blood calcium levels.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Parathyroid Gland and Calcium Balance'.
questions.a: PTH and TCT act antagonistically to maintain calcium homeostasis in the blood.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Parathyroid Gland and Calcium Balance' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.2.5 (source: kebo119.txt lines 190-205)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Adrenal Gland and Stress Response' refers to.
questions.a: Glands located above the kidneys consisting of a medulla (secreting emergency hormones) and a cortex (secreting corticoids).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Adrenal Gland and Stress Response'.
questions.a: The adrenal gland manages both immediate stress (medulla) and long-term metabolic/electrolyte balance (cortex).

questions.q: Under which section is 'Adrenal Gland and Stress Response' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.2.7 (source: kebo119.txt lines 215-260)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Pancreas and Glucose Homeostasis' refers to.
questions.a: A composite gland containing Islets of Langerhans that secrete insulin and glucagon to manage blood sugar.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Pancreas and Glucose Homeostasis'.
questions.a: Insulin (hypoglycemic) and glucagon (hyperglycemic) maintain stable blood glucose levels.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Pancreas and Glucose Homeostasis' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.2.8 (source: kebo119.txt lines 265-295)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mechanism of Hormone Action' refers to.
questions.a: The process where hormones bind to specific receptors to trigger biochemical changes and physiological responses in target tissues.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mechanism of Hormone Action'.
questions.a: Water-soluble hormones use second messengers, while lipid-soluble hormones regulate gene expression directly.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Mechanism of Hormone Action' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 19.4 (source: kebo119.txt lines 345-375)
